content: Atriplex, commonly referred to as saltbush or orache, is a genus of plants encompassing between 100 and 200 species. These plants are highly diverse and are found in a wide range of environments, including deserts, seashores, and moist habitats. Many species within this genus are halophytes, meaning they are adapted to thrive in saline conditions. The genus Atriplex is classified under the goosefoot subfamily (Chenopodioideae) of the Amaranthaceae family, though it was previously considered part of the distinct family Chenopodiaceae. The name Atriplex originates from Latin and was historically used by Pliny the Elder to describe edible oraches. Saltbush plants are particularly notable for their ability to tolerate high salt concentrations in the soil. They achieve this by retaining salt in their leaves, which makes them valuable in areas affected by soil salinization. Additionally, Atriplex species serve as food sources for the larvae of certain Lepidoptera species and provide shelter and hunting grounds for spiders like Phidippus californicus and other arthropods in otherwise barren habitats. Many Atriplex species are edible, with the most commonly consumed species being Garden Orache (Atriplex hortensis). The use of Atriplex as a food source dates back to at least the late Epipaleolithic (Mesolithic) period. For example, the Ertebølle culture likely used Common Orache (Atriplex patula) as a vegetable, as evidenced by its presence as an archaeophyte in northern Europe. In the biblical Book of Job, the term mallûḥa (מַלּ֣וּחַ), likely referring to Mediterranean Saltbush (Atriplex halimus), is mentioned as food consumed by social outcasts. In Australia, Grey Saltbush (Atriplex cinerea) has been used as bush food since prehistoric times. Native Americans consumed species such as Chamisso (Atriplex canescens) and Shadscale (Atriplex confertifolia), while Spearscale (Atriplex hastata) was a food source in rural Eurasia. Garden Orache (Atriplex hortensis), also known as Red Orache, Mountain Spinach, or French Spinach, is an annual leafy vegetable with a salty, spinach-like flavor. It grows to a height of 1–2 meters (3–6 feet), and its leaves can be consumed either cooked or raw in salads. Historically, it was widely cultivated in Mediterranean regions until spinach became the preferred leafy vegetable. The leaves of Garden Orache come in red, white, and green varieties, with the green leaves once being used to color pasta in Italy. Orache is also commonly used to balance the acidic flavor of sorrel in culinary applications. Sheep that graze on saltbush produce meat with surprisingly high levels of vitamin E. This meat is leaner, more hydrated, and has consumer appeal comparable to grain-fed lamb. The elevated vitamin E levels may provide health benefits to the animals while also extending the shelf life and maintaining the fresh red color of the meat. This effect has been demonstrated in species such as Old Man Saltbush (Atriplex nummularia) and River Saltbush (Atriplex amnicola). Interestingly, sheep appear to prefer the more fibrous and less nutritious River Saltbush for reasons that remain unclear. Saltbushes are also used as ornamental plants in landscaping and are effective in preventing soil erosion in coastal areas. Old Man Saltbush has been successfully employed in the rehabilitation of old mining sites, such as those around Lightning Ridge in Australia.
